metadata.title: Willy v. Coastal Corp., 503 U.S. 131 (1992) (No. 90-1150)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Willy v. Coastal Corp.

Opinion filed: 1992-03-03

Docket No.: 90-1150

Citations:
• 117 L. Ed. 2d 280
• 112 S. Ct. 1076
• 503 U.S. 131
• 1992 U.S. LEXIS 1521

Case holding summaries:
• upholding a Rule 11 award following dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
• “A final determination of lack of subject-matter jurisdiction of a case in a federal court, of course, pre- cludes further adjudication of it.”
• holding that a district court had jurisdiction to impose Rule 11 sanctions regardless of the existence of subject-matter jurisdiction
• "[I]t is well established that a federal court may consider collateral issues after an action is no longer pending. . . . Such an order implicates no constitutional concern because it does not signify a district court's assessment of the legal merits of the complaint."
• "Rule 11 appl[ies] to all district court proceedings"
• court can impose Rule 11 sanctions even if, in retrospect, it lacked subject matter jurisdiction over merits of the case
• in holding that a court may impose Rule 11 sanctions in a case in which it is later determined the court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction, the Court noted " '[i]t is well established that a federal court may consider collateral issues after an action is no longer pending.' "
• imposition of Rule 11 sanctions is not an adjudication on the merits and, therefore, "does not raise the issue of a district court adjudicating the merits of a 'case or controversy' over which it lacks jurisdiction"
• holding federal district courts may impose Rule 11 sanctions even “in a case in which the district court is later determined to be without sub- ject-matter jurisdiction”
• upholding FED. R. CIV. P. 11 sanctions even though the district court eventually concluded that it lacked Article III jurisdiction
• declining to apply 1993 amendments, which became effective during pendency of appeal
• civil contempt is designed to force contemnor to comply with direct order of court
• sanctions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11, allowed even though case dismissed for want of subject matter jurisdiction
• Rule 11 sanctions allowed even when court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over the underlying case
• holding that a district court had jurisdiction to impose Rule 11 sanctions even though it was later found to lack jurisdiction over the underlying case
• "The interest in having rules of procedure obeyed ... does not disappear upon a subsequent determination that the court was without subject-matter jurisdiction."
• addressing sanctions under Rule 11
• affirming district court’s imposition of Rule 11 sanctions despite lack of subject matter jurisdiction
• upholding Rule 11 sanctions imposed where the district court lacked jurisdiction
• noting that it is the "clear intent to have the [Federal] Rules [of Civil Procedure], including Rule 11, apply to all district court proceedings"
• need for finality in litigation justifies a rule against collateral attacks on subject matter jurisdiction
• because an imposition of Fed.R.Civ.P. 11 sanctions concerns a party's violation of the court's rules and does not entail a judgment on the merits, a court may rule on a sanctions motion even though it has determined that it was without subject matter jurisdiction
• sanctions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 , allowed even though case dismissed for want of subject matter jurisdiction
• upholding Rule 11 sanctions in a case in which the district court was later found to lack subject matter jurisdiction because the sanctions order did not “raise the issue of a district court adjudicating the merits of a ‘case or controversy’ over which it lacks jurisdiction”
• noting that "[a] final determination of lack of subject-matter jurisdiction of a case in a federal court, of course, precludes further adjudication of it."
• discussing Article III-based limits on court's ability to impose sanctions where court never had subject matter jurisdiction
• affirming imposition of Rule 11 sanctions even when it was later determined that district court lacked subject matter jurisdiction
• noting that “[i]t is well established that a federal court may consider collateral issues after an action is no longer pending” (quotation omitted)
• discussing Article III-based limits on court’s ability to impose sanctions where court never had subject matter jurisdiction
• “The interest in having rules of procedure obeyed . . . does not disappear upon a subsequent determination that the court was without subject-matter jurisdiction.”
• explaining that the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, pursuant to the language in Rule 81(c), “govern procedure after removal”
• affirming a Rule 11 sanction imposed jointly and severally on both client and attorney
• holding that the district court had the authority to impose sanctions pursuant to Fed.R.Civ.P. 11 in a case in which it later determined that it lacked subject matter jurisdiction
• “Such an order implicates no constitutional concern because it does not signify a district court’s assessment of the legal merits of the complaint.” (quotation omitted)
• "Given that civil contempt is designed to coerce compliance with the court's decree, it is logical that the [contempt] order itself should fall with a showing that the court was without authority to enter the [underlying] decree."
• finding that even where a -4- Case No. 19-2460, Howlett v. City of Warren federal court lacks jurisdiction over a case, it retains the power to impose sanctions for violations of federal rules
• holding that a district court’s power to sanction survives lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
• holding that a district court acts within the scope valid federal procedures in imposing Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 sanctions after it has been determined that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction over a case
• holding that a district court can impose Rule 11 sanctions “in a case in which the district court is later determined to be without subject-matter jurisdiction”
• holding that a court has jurisdiction to make orders necessary for “the maintenance of orderly procedure,” including the issuance of sanctions against attorneys, even if its determination of its jurisdiction over the underlying action later turns out to be mistaken
• “[T]he practical concern with providing an end to litigation justifies a rule preventing collateral attack on subject-matter jurisdiction.”
• holding that district court had authority to issue Rule 11 sanctions for conduct in case ultimately dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
• upholding Rule 11 sanctions 19 before court of appeals determined district court lacked subject 20 matter jurisdiction
